extracted.intended_audience: students of literature, critics, and novelists interested in craft
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for constructing and judging the novel, emphasizing the difference between story and plot, the requirements of plot (intelligence, memory, mystery, economy), the balance between character and plot, and the separate demands of fantasy/prophecy. Draws on examples (Meredith, Hardy, Gide, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Story vs Plot (time-sequence vs causality)
rubrics_metrics.description: The story preserves time-sequence: 'and then?'. The plot emphasizes causality and asks 'why?'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the distinction to decide whether your work is serving mere curiosity (a story) or engaging the reader's intelligence and memory (a plot). Examples: 'The queen died of grief' as a plot (asks why) vs simple sequence. A plot cannot be appreciated by audiences who only supply curiosity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot requires intelligence
rubrics_metrics.description: Curiosity alone is insufficient; the plot demands intelligence — the reader must mentally pick up facts, relate them to previous pages, and hold uncertainties for later understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include cross-correspondences and material whose full meaning dawns later (detective/mystery element). Avoid relying on mere 'and then—and then' sequencing if you want a plotful reader experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot requires memory
rubrics_metrics.description: Unless the reader remembers earlier facts (persons, events), causal chains cannot be understood; the plot-maker expects the reader to remember and expects no loose ends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure actions and words recur coherently, leave no unresolved threads; design incidents so readers can rearrange and reconsider earlier clues toward a final sense. Anti-pattern: assuming reader forgetfulness will still allow understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mystery as essential element of plot
rubrics_metrics.description: Mystery (a suspension of time-sequence, a 'pocket in time')—from crude 'Why did the queen die?' to subtle half-explained gestures—is essential to a plot and requires intelligence to appreciate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use mystery to create pockets of withheld knowledge that pay off later; ensure mysteries are solvable by the reader's memory/intelligence rather than mere tricks. Avoid mysteries that only produce 'and then' curiosity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy and organic unity
rubrics_metrics.description: Every action or word ought to count; the plot should be economical and spare, organic and free from dead matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trim incidental dead matter; make events and dialogue contribute to the causal/ thematic whole. Scoring note: excess padding or irrelevant episodes weaken the plot's integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not mislead the reader
rubrics_metrics.description: A plot 'ought not to mislead' — clues and incidents should not intentionally deceive unless ethically or artistically justified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you misdirect, ensure the misdirection is fair and contributes to the aesthetic unity rather than cheap surprise. Anti-pattern: arbitrary trickery that betrays the reader's investment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surprise balanced with plausibility
rubrics_metrics.description: A plot ought to cause surprise (the shock followed by 'Oh, that's all right') while preserving believable character behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for incidents that are unexpected yet consistent with what has been established about characters and world. Example: Meredith's contrivances cause delightful shocks that also make sense in retrospect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contrivance as a legitimate device (when organic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Contrivances (devices or doors through which a book passes and emerges altered) are acceptable when they spring from character and react upon them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use contrivances that grow out of established character motivation; avoid contrivances that feel artificial or externally imposed. Example: Meredith's horse-whipping incident transforms the book without destroying plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Withholding information must respect character integrity
rubrics_metrics.description: Concealing a character's inner change (to enhance plot surprise) can be effective but risks damaging perceived integrity if it contradicts prior narrative voice or promises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justify suppressed information ethically within the narration. Example: Meredith conceals Laetitia's change for comic effect; Charlotte Brontë's concealment in Villette produces a thrill but slightly harms Lucy Snowe's integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid plot domination that sacrifices character reality
rubrics_metrics.description: When plot triumphs too completely, characters may have to suspend their natures or be swept by fate, weakening their reality and vitality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance causal design and human complexity. Critics of Hardy: strong emphasis on causality can canalize characters into roles that feel thin or impoverished. Strive for characters who can act independently of the plot when necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of mechanical endings and winding-up
rubrics_metrics.description: Many novels 'go off at the end' because the plot must be wound up; authors resort to stock solutions (death, marriage) or the characters go dead while the author finishes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid contrived dénouements and overreliance on conventional finales. Maintain character momentum through the close; watch for a loss of 'pep' or the author's overbearing logic replacing living action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Planning (plotting) vs organic growth
rubrics_metrics.description: Question whether a novel should be pre-planned (plot as a logical framework) or allowed to grow (author subdued by reality), as advocated by Gide's method of no plan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose an approach suited to the novel's aims: plotting gives logical causality and mystery; growth may open space for subconscious, fantasy, or wider inclusions. Be aware each method makes different demands on the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fantasy's additional demand on the reader
rubrics_metrics.description: Fantasy asks readers to 'pay something extra': accept the book as a whole and accept certain extraordinary things within it; it may require acceptance of the supernatural or its absence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce fantastic elements only insofar as they are suitable to the book; recognize many readers will reject the additional adjustment. The fantastic's success depends on the book's internal laws and tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish fantasy from prophecy (mythologies differ)
rubrics_metrics.description: Both fantasy and prophecy use mythologies ('gods'), but the gods differ: fantasy summons smaller, mischievous, improvisatory deities (Hermes-like), while prophecy invokes transcendent, often tragic deities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the appropriate mythic register: fantasy tends toward improv, sideshow charm, and small-scale enchantments; prophetic novels aim for grandeur and transcendence. Misregistering tone and myth weakens the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability of the fantastic to the novel's general tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Once in the fictive realm, any element may be true if it suits the book, but the general 'literal' tone of most novels makes the fantastic demand an extra concession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether an angel, ghost, or other fantastic element harmonizes with established tone and reader expectations. If the fantastic is mismatched, readers may stop or read coldly, undermining engagement.
